semantic_correction.stem: A client receiving hemodialysis has been prescribed a fluid restriction. Which statement shows correct understanding of fluid-management teaching?

options.A: I will count foods that are liquid at room temperature, such as soup, gelatin, pudding, and ice cream, toward my fluid intake and limit excess sodium that can increase thirst.
options.B: I will count beverages toward my fluid limit but exclude gelatin, pudding, and ice cream because foods eaten with a spoon do not contribute meaningful fluid.
options.C: I can increase my fluid intake on days without ankle swelling because visible edema is the best indicator of whether extra fluid is safe between treatments.
options.D: I will add more salty foods when I feel thirsty because sodium helps retain fluid inside the circulation and makes a fluid restriction easier to tolerate.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases guidance for people receiving hemodialysis states that foods that are liquid at room temperature, including soup, gelatin, pudding, and ice cream, count toward total fluid intake. NIDDK also explains that excess fluid between treatments can contribute to swelling, blood-pressure changes, cardiac strain, and fluid in the lungs. Sodium can increase thirst, so reducing excess salt helps make fluid restriction easier to follow. Therefore the client should count liquid-containing foods and limit excess sodium as part of the prescribed fluid-management plan. B is incorrect because several foods eaten with a spoon still contribute to total fluid intake. C is incorrect because absence of visible ankle edema does not replace the individualized fluid prescription or target-weight plan. D is incorrect because sodium tends to increase thirst and can worsen fluid-management difficulty rather than reduce it.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients receiving hemodialysis to count liquid-containing foods toward prescribed fluid intake and limit excess sodium because salt increases thirst and excess fluid can contribute to clinically important volume complications.
semantic_correction.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), National Institutes of Health
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current NIDDK hemodialysis nutrition guidance verified August 23, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Why is it important to keep track of how much liquid I eat or drink?: excess fluid between treatments can contribute to swelling, blood-pressure changes, cardiac strain, and fluid in the lungs; salt increases thirst. What foods count as liquid and why?: foods liquid at room temperature such as soup, gelatin, pudding, and ice cream count toward total fluid intake.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current NIDDK guidance directly supports counting liquid-at-room-temperature foods toward total fluid intake and limiting excess sodium because salt increases thirst and excess fluid between dialysis treatments can cause volume-related complications.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the answer-length cue, rebuilt all four client statements to comparable length and specificity, freshly verified current NIDDK hemodialysis fluid-management guidance, and preserved liquid-food counting plus sodium reduction as the single best response.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests practical hemodialysis fluid-restriction teaching with one clearly best statement, balanced alternatives, current NIDDK guidance, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It directly matches NIDDK guidance on counting liquid foods and limiting sodium to reduce thirst and fluid-management difficulty.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Gelatin, pudding, ice cream, and similar foods contribute to total fluid intake even though they are eaten with a spoon.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Visible edema alone is not an adequate basis for changing a prescribed fluid restriction between dialysis treatments.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Sodium increases thirst and can make fluid restriction and interdialytic fluid control more difficult.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely combines both source-supported self-management principles; B undercounts fluid, C substitutes edema for the prescribed plan, and D reverses the sodium-thirst relationship.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel client statements of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed.
